passages.original: 7. Nam Latinorum interpretum, qui de Græco in nostrum eloquium transtulerunt (ut meminit sanctus Augustinus [u de Doctr. Christ. c. 11]) infinitus nuMerus. Sicut enim (inquit) primis fidei temporibus ad manus venit Codex Graecus, atque aliquantulum sibi utriusque linguae peritiam sumpsit, ausus est statim interpretari, atque inde accidit tam innu* merabiles apud Latinos exstitisse interpretes.
passages.english: 7. For the number of Latin translators who have rendered [the Scriptures] from Greek into our language is, as Saint Augustine recalls, beyond counting. "For," he says, "in the first times of the faith, whenever a Greek codex came into anyone's hands and he thought he had acquired a little skill in both languages, he at once ventured to translate, and so it came about that there arose such countless translators among the Latins."
passages.notes: The bracketed reference "u de Doctr. Christ. c. 11" is an editorial citation (Augustine, On Christian Doctrine 2.11) and is omitted; the "u" is likely a footnote mark. "Sicut... ad manus venit" is read in the sense of Augustine's "ut cuique" ("whenever... came into anyone's hands"); the Latin as printed lacks an explicit subject.

passages.original: Quae et ipsa a nonnullis ejus esse negatur, sed sub nomine ejns ab alio dictata existimatur. Joannis epistolas tres idem Joanocs edidit, quarum prima tantum a quibusdam ejus esse asseritur, reliqua duæ Joannis cujusdam presbyteri existimantur, cujus juxta Hieronymi sententiam alterum sepulcrum apud Ephesum demonstratur. Judas suam edidit Epistolam. Actus apostulorum Lucas composuit, sicut audivit, vel vidit. Apocalypsin Joaunes evangelista scripsit eodem tempore, quo ob Evangelii praedicationem in insulam Pathmos traditur relegatis.
passages.english: This too is denied by some to be his, and is thought to have been composed by another under his name. The same John issued three epistles, of which only the first is asserted by some to be his; the other two are thought to belong to a certain John the presbyter, whose second tomb, according to Jerome's view, is shown at Ephesus. Jude issued his Epistle. Luke composed the Acts of the Apostles as he heard or saw [the events]. John the Evangelist wrote the Apocalypse at the same time as he is reported to have been banished to the island of Patmos for preaching the Gospel.
passages.notes: "Quae et ipsa" refers to a work named before the passage (probably the Epistle of James, named in the preceding context). "relegatis" is read as "relegatus".

passages.original: 4. Hæc autem dem sunt visibilia, sanctificata tamen per Spiritum sanctum 384 in sacramentum divini corporis transeant. Proinde autem, ut sanctissimus Cyprianus ait: < Calix dominicus vino et aqua mistus offertur, quia videmus in aqua populum intelligi, in vino vero ostendi sanguinem Christi. Quando autem in calice fino aqoa miscetur, Christo populus adunatur, et eredentium plebs ei in quern credidit copulatur et jungitur. Quæ copulatio et conjunctio aquae et vini sic miscetnr In calice Domini, ut commistio illa ab invicem non possit separari, sicut nec Ecclesia potest a Christo dividi.
passages.english: 4. These, then, are visible things, yet when sanctified through the Holy Spirit they pass into the sacrament of the divine body. Accordingly, as the most holy Cyprian says: "The Lord's cup is offered mixed with wine and water, because we see that the people is understood in the water, while in the wine the blood of Christ is shown. And when water is mixed with wine in the cup, the people is united to Christ, and the multitude of believers is coupled and joined to him in whom it has believed. This coupling and joining of water and wine is so mingled in the Lord's cup that that mixture cannot be separated, just as the Church cannot be divided from Christ."
passages.notes: "dem" is read as "quidem" or "eadem"; "transeant" is translated in the sense of "transeunt". The numeral 384 is a page number and is omitted.

passages.original: Nam et cum Dominus dicit : Qui peccaverit in Spiritum sanctum, non remittetur ei, nec in hoc sæculo, nec futuro (Matth, XII), demonstrat quibusdam illic dimittenda peccata et quodam purgatorio igne purganda. Ergo in quodam loco dictum est a san- etissimo Augustino : < Defunctorum animas sine dubio pietate suoram viventium relevari, eum pro illis sacrificium offertur, vel eleemosynae fiunt, si tamen aliquod quisque sibi meritum preparavit, dum adhuc in corpore viveret, per quod ista prosint, qua cunque pro illo fiunt.
passages.english: For when the Lord also says, "Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, either in this age or in the age to come" (Matthew 12), he shows that for some people sins are to be forgiven there and cleansed by a kind of purgatorial fire. So in a certain place it is said by the most holy Augustine: "The souls of the dead are without doubt relieved by the piety of their living [kin], when the sacrifice is offered for them or alms are given, provided, however, that each person prepared for himself some merit while he was still living in the body, through which whatever is done for him may benefit him."

passages.original: 1.De matutinorum antiquitate et auctoritate testis est idem David propheta, dicens : In matutinis meditabor in te, quia fuisti adjutor meus, et alibi : Prævenerunt, inquit, oculi mei ad te diluculo, ut meditarer eloquia tua. Cassianus autem dicit matutinae 390 solemnitatis officium novo adhuc tempore institutum primitus in Belhlehem monasterio, ubi Dominus noster Jesus Christus pro redemptione humani generis ex virine nasci dignatus est.
passages.english: 1. On the antiquity and authority of Matins the same prophet David is a witness, saying, "In the morning I will meditate on you, because you have been my helper," and elsewhere, "My eyes," he says, "went before [the dawn] to you at daybreak, that I might meditate on your words." Cassian, however, says that the office of the morning solemnity was instituted only recently, first in the monastery at Bethlehem, where our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to be born of a virgin for the redemption of the human race.
passages.notes: The numeral 390 is a page number and is omitted.

passages.original: 3. Refert autem Cassianus apud ÆgyptiosNativitatis diem, 394 et epiphaniorum solemnitatem non bifarie, ut in occiduis provinciis, sed sub diei .Ains festivitate celebrari. Epistolæ quoque pontificis Alexandrini per universas Ægypti Ecelesia. vel monasteria diriguntur, quibus et initium Quadragesimæ, et dies Pasehæ denuntiatur.
passages.english: 3. Cassian reports that among the Egyptians the day of the Nativity and the solemnity of the Epiphany are celebrated not separately, as in the western provinces, but under the festival of a single day. Letters of the bishop of Alexandria are also sent to all the churches and monasteries of Egypt, by which both the beginning of Lent and the day of Easter are announced.
passages.notes: "sub diei .Ains festivitate" is read as "sub diei unius festivitate" ("under the festival of a single day"). The numeral 394 is a page number and is omitted.

passages.original: 5. Cujus quidem Quadragesimæ lege, sicut ait noster Cassianus, quique perfecti sunt non tenentur, nec exigui hujus canonis subjectione contenti sunt. Quem profecto illis qui per totum anni spatium deli- eiis ae negotiis seccularibus implicantur, Ecclesiarum , principes statuerunt, ut, vel hac legali quodammodo necessitate constricti, his saltem diebus vacare Domino cogerentur, ac dierum vitæ suae, quos totos quasi quosdam fructus fuerant voraturi, velut decimas Domino dedicarent.
passages.english: 5. By the law of this Lent, as our Cassian says, those who are perfect are not bound, nor are they content with submission to this slight rule. The leaders of the churches established it, surely, for those who throughout the whole course of the year are entangled in pleasures and worldly business, so that, constrained at least by this quasi-legal necessity, they might be compelled on these days at any rate to have leisure for the Lord, and might dedicate to the Lord, as tithes, [some] of the days of their life, all of which they had been about to devour like so much produce.

passages.original: 5. Quartum genus est qui sibi anachoretarum imagine blandiuntur; isti, ut ait Cassianus, in primordiis nil fervore quodam brevi cænobii perfectionem videntur expetere, sed continuo tepefacti, dum pristinos mores ac vitia resecare contemnunt, nee jugum humilitatis ac patientiæ diutius sustinere contenti sunt, subdique seniorum imperio dedignantur, separatas expetunt cellas, ac solitarii sedere dcsiderant, ut a nemine lacessiti, mansueti vel humiles existimentur, quae institutio, imo tepor, hos quos semel infecerit ad perfectionem nunquam permittit accedere.
passages.english: 5. The fourth kind consists of those who flatter themselves with the semblance of anchorites. These, as Cassian says, seem at the beginning to seek the perfection of the monastery with a certain brief fervour, but they soon grow lukewarm. Since they disdain to cut away their former habits and vices, are not content to bear the yoke of humility and patience any longer, and scorn to be subject to the authority of the elders, they seek separate cells and wish to sit alone, so that, provoked by no one, they may be thought gentle or humble. This way of life, or rather lukewarmness, never allows those whom it has once infected to approach perfection.
passages.notes: "nil" before "fervore" is read as "nam" or as an intrusion; it is left untranslated.

passages.original: Construunt enim sibi cellulas, easque falso nomine monasteria nuncupant, liberique ab imperio seniorum, arbilrio suo vivunt. certatim in operibus laborantes, non ut indigentibus distribuant, sed ut acquirant pecunias, quas recondant. et sicut ait de ipsis Hieronymus, quasi ars sit sancta, non vita, quidquid vendiderint, majoris est pretii.
passages.english: For they build themselves little cells and call them by the false name of monasteries. Free from the authority of the elders, they live by their own will, labouring competitively at their handiwork, not to distribute [the proceeds] to the needy, but to acquire money to hoard. And as Jerome says of them, as though their craft, not their life, were holy, whatever they sell fetches a higher price.

passages.original: Sacramentum autem ideo inter conjugatos dictum est, quia sicut non potest Ecclesia dividi a Christo, ita et uxor a viro (Ephes. v). Quod ergo in , Christo et in Ecclesia , hoc in singulis quibusque viris atque uxoribus conjunctionis inseparahile Sacramentum est. Unde et Apostolus : Præcipio, inquit, non ego, sed Dominus, uxorem a viro non discedere (I Cor. vu). Prohibet enim dimitti quacunque ex causa , ne aliis conjungatur secundum consuetudinem Judxorum, quam Dominus interdixit, dicens: Quicunque dimiserit uxorem suam, excepta fornicatianis causa , et aliam duxerit, moechatur (Matth. XIX). Solum (ut ait Hieronymus) adulterium est, quod uxoris vincat affectum, imo cum illa unam carnem in aliam diviserit, et se fornicatione separaverit, a marito non debet teneri, ne virum quoque sub ma- Jediclo faciat, dicente Scriptura : Qui adulteram te- net, stultus et impius eat (Proverb. XVIII). Ubicunque igitur fornicatio est, et fornicationis suspicio, libere uxor dimittitur.
passages.english: Marriage between spouses is called a sacrament for this reason: just as the Church cannot be divided from Christ, so neither can a wife from her husband (Ephesians 5). What, then, [holds] in Christ and in the Church is, in each husband and wife, the inseparable sacrament of union. Hence the Apostle also says: "I command, not I but the Lord, that a wife not depart from her husband" (1 Corinthians 7). For he forbids her to be put away for any cause whatever, lest she be joined to others according to the custom of the Jews, which the Lord forbade, saying: "Whoever puts away his wife, except for the cause of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery" (Matthew 19). Only adultery, as Jerome says, is [a thing] that overcomes affection for a wife. Indeed, when she has divided one flesh into another and separated herself by fornication, she ought not to be kept by her husband, lest she bring the husband too under a curse, as Scripture says: "He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious" (Proverbs 18). Wherever, therefore, there is fornication, or suspicion of fornication, a wife is freely put away.
passages.notes: "stultus et impius eat" is read as "est".

passages.original: Quid ergo, si sterilis est, si deformis, si ætate vetula, si fetida , si temulenta , si iracunda, si malis moribus, si luxuriosa, si fatua, si gulosa, si vaga, si jurgatrix et maledica? tenenda est, 457 velis, nolis , et qualiscunque accepta , est habenda. Cum enim esses liber, sponte te servituti subjecisti. Cumque habet quis uxorem (ut ait Lactantius ), neque servam, neque liberam habere poterit, ut matrimon'i fidem servet. Neque enim , ut juris publici ratio est, sola mulier adultera est quae, virum habens, ab altero polluitur, et maritus, si alteram habeat, a crimine adulterii alienus habeatur, dum divina lex duos ita in unum matrimonii corpus conjunxerit, ut adulter sit quisquis compagem corporis in diversa distraxerit.
passages.english: What then, if she is barren, if she is ugly, if she is old in years, if she smells foul, if she is a drunkard, if she is quick to anger, if she is of bad character, if she is lustful, if she is foolish, if she is gluttonous, if she is a wanderer, if she is quarrelsome and abusive? She must be kept, whether you will or not, and whatever sort of woman she was when taken, she must be held to. For when you were free, you of your own accord subjected yourself to servitude. And when anyone has a wife (as Lactantius says), he may not have either a slave woman or a free woman, so that he may keep the faith of marriage. For it is not the case, as the reckoning of public law has it, that only the woman is an adulteress who, having a husband, is defiled by another, while the husband, if he has another woman, is held to be free of the charge of adultery; since the divine law has so joined the two into one body of marriage that whoever pulls the union of the body apart in different directions is an adulterer.
passages.notes: The numeral '457' in the text is a page number from the printed edition and has been omitted. 'matrimon'i' is read as 'matrimonii'.
